title: Now states are mandating recess. Really?
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Mike Petrilli uses the growing push for state recess mandates to ask a broader question about education governance: when should federal, state, district, school or teacher decision makers make the call? He is sympathetic to recess but agrees with Chad Aldis that states setting minimum times for every subject produces a one-size-fits-all squeeze on the school day. He proposes three conditions for state dictates: overwhelming evidence, easy implementation and enforcement, and an intractable local barrier. The rest of the issue is a policy roundup covering reactions to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit regulations, including Jon Valant’s prediction that it becomes a regressive source of funding, and a three-way Education Next debate on education savings accounts. He also surveys reactions to season two of Sold a Story, which spotlights Direct Instruction, and closes with Wisconsin voices who see hope for cross-sector school choice and accountability.
points: Petrilli reframes the recess debate as a who-decides question, and offers three tests for state mandates: overwhelming evidence, easy enforcement, and an intractable local barrier.
Chad Aldis’s objection is that recess, math and reading all deserve time, so lawmakers who set minimums for each need to reckon with how long the school day actually is.

Valant and others warn that the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit could fund wealthy counties at several times the per-child rate of poor ones, because donors and tax liability cluster in affluent places.
The Education Next ESA forum splits into pro, anti and Ashley Berner’s middle view that ESAs expand pluralism but do nothing about academic rigor or public outcome reporting.

Reactions to Sold a Story season two converge on the point that schools matter and effective teaching helps students, while Natalie Wexler warns against concluding that Direct Instruction alone solves everything.
quotes: A recurring question here at SCHOOLED, and in education policy writ large, comes down not to the what but to the who. In other words, for any policy decision related to education, when is it appropriate for the feds, state government, local school districts, individual schools, or individual teachers to make the call?

If states are going to set minimum times for everything, please give lawmakers a calculator and a basic understanding of how long the day is. The reading blocks in many states are crazy long. Intervention in many states requires an additional 30 to 60 minutes if a student is below grade level.
Changing state law is of course an option, but it creates a one-size-fits-all approach. For Ohio, that means 600+ districts must allocate time the same way. You better be sure that you’re right.
It seems much likelier that we come to see the FSTC as a Title I for rich kids than a source of redistributive, charitable giving.
An ESA empowers them. This isn’t just a policy tweak. It signifies a fundamental shift in the power dynamic—one that puts families rather than institutions in control.

The season’s real, insistent lesson is this: schools matter, and students do better when educators teach more effectively. Yes, poverty and health and nutrition and other structural forces also affect children’s development.

Americans may be increasingly critical of higher education without being ready to give up on it. People can believe that college is too expensive, too political, overrated or no longer worth what it costs—and still believe that a college degree is the best bet for themselves or their own children.
